title: Testing Didn't Ruin School. Nostalgia Ruined the Conversation.
author: uglylearning
summary: The Ugly Learning newsletter argues that the dominant narrative in education criticism -- that standardized testing ruined schools that were previously excellent -- is empirically dishonest and intellectually irresponsible. The piece makes three arguments. First, the schools being remembered as excellent served a very different population: graduation rates in 1960 were under 70%, meaning the 'excellent schools' of living memory were excellent for the students who completed them, but a large minority never made it through. Second, composition changes in the student population (more students from lower-income families, more English language learners, more students with disabilities) account for a substantial portion of the measured decline in average test scores. Third, the nostalgia narrative misdirects reform: if the problem is 'testing ruined good schools,' the solution is to remove testing; if the problem is 'we are now serving a much more diverse and challenging population,' the solution is very different.
points: * Graduation rates in 1960 were under 70%, meaning the 'excellent schools' of nostalgic memory were selectively excellent -- they served a population screened by the high dropout rate that preceded the measures being remembered as evidence of quality. * Composition changes in the student population -- more students from lower-income families, more English language learners, more students with disabilities -- account for a substantial portion of measured declines in average test scores. * The nostalgia narrative misdirects reform: if testing ruined good schools, remove testing; if the challenge is serving a more diverse and historically underserved population, the solution requires investment in instructional quality, not removal of accountability. * The piece makes an explicit argument about intellectual honesty in education criticism: claiming schools were better before testing is only defensible if you acknowledge who was in schools before testing and who was not. * The implication for current education debates is that 'going back to how schools used to be' is not a neutral nostalgic preference but a proposal to return to a system that served a narrower and more privileged population.
quotes: The schools people remember as excellent were excellent. For the people who made it through them. The graduation rate in 1960 was somewhere around 65 to 70%. The students who experienced those schools as excellent were not experiencing a typical education. They were experiencing the education that the selection effect of a 30% dropout rate had filtered them into.

When you account for composition changes -- for the expansion of special education, for the growth of English language learner populations, for the shift in the socioeconomic distribution of students completing K-12 -- much of the apparent decline in school quality disappears. The schools are serving harder cases. The averages reflect that.

The 'testing ruined schools' narrative is the most consequential version of the nostalgia problem because it prescribes a reform: remove accountability, return to teacher autonomy, and schools will be good again. That prescription only makes sense if the premise is correct. The premise is not correct.

I am not defending the specific testing regimes of the past twenty years. Many of them were badly designed, badly implemented, and badly used. But the critique of specific implementations is different from the claim that accountability itself destroyed something that was previously excellent. The latter is an empirical claim, and the evidence doesn't support it.

The honest version of the nostalgia argument goes like this: we had excellent schools for the students we chose to keep. We have worse average outcomes now because we are keeping more students and serving more of their needs. That is a challenge that deserves investment, not a decline that deserves a scapegoat.
